claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading in FCC/BCC HEA multilayers is governed jointly by interface-mediated dislocation nucleation and enhanced atomic diffusion at chemically complex, lattice-distorted interfaces.
Coherent, lattice-mismatched interfaces are lower-activation-energy sites for dislocation emission and diffusion-assisted climb.
Interface-mediated dislocation emission and diffusion-assisted climb enable progressive plastic strain while balancing strength and deformation tolerance.
The proposed starting coatings contain alternating nanoscale FCC and BCC HEA layers with sharply defined, coherent interfaces.
Reducing individual layer thickness while retaining total architecture will increase or otherwise modify FCC/BCC interface density and character.
Chemical inhomogeneity and lattice-misfit strain at FCC/BCC interfaces generate local stress fields.
The interfacial local stress fields facilitate dislocation nucleation.
The interfaces promote atomic diffusion associated with dislocation climb.
Under sustained loading, stored elastic energy concentrates at coherent, distorted interfaces.
Interfacial elastic-energy concentration promotes progressive dislocation nucleation.
Atomic diffusion facilitates dislocation climb across FCC/BCC interfaces and thereby redistributes strain.
Combined interfacial nucleation and diffusion-assisted climb produce gradual, stable plastic-strain accumulation without premature catastrophic failure.
Reduced-layer-thickness multilayers should have a lower effective creep activation volume than the thicker-layer baseline.
Reduced-layer-thickness multilayers should accumulate plastic strain more uniformly and progressively than the thicker-layer baseline.
Reduced-layer-thickness multilayers should show greater interfacial dislocation density and more diffusion-accommodated interface activity in TEM.
Reduced-layer-thickness multilayers should have a lower apparent creep rate near the yield stress and steadier strain progression than the thicker-layer baseline.
Interface-mediated processes dominate when individual layer dimensions are on the order of tens of nanometers.
The relative contributions of dislocation nucleation and diffusion are sensitive to temperature and applied stress.
Keeping total thickness and overall composition fixed while changing layer thickness provides a controlled comparison of interface-density effects.
Failure of thinner-layer samples to show the predicted activation-volume, creep, and interfacial-activity changes would falsify the proposed interface-controlled mechanism.
